subsystems.name: Trigger sensor
subsystems.role: detects what the colour should respond to — temperature, a blood chemical, or a wireless command.

subsystems.name: Colour element
subsystems.role: the part that actually changes appearance.
parts: engineered pigment cells (melanocytes or chromatophore-like cells)

subsystems.name: Control and power
subsystems.role: decides when to switch and supplies the small current needed.
parts: near-field (NFC) coil for wireless power and data

subsystems.name: Encapsulation
subsystems.role: keeps the device from being attacked by the immune system and keeps its contents inside.

subsystems.name: Delivery and placement
subsystems.role: gets the material into the dermis without surgery where possible.

subsystems.name: External reader
subsystems.role: a phone or wearable that sends commands, supplies power and reads back state.

buildSteps.title: Pick the trigger and colour mechanism
buildSteps.detail: A change in temperature, pH, glucose or an incoming radio command is paired with a material that visibly responds — electrochromic for electrical control, thermochromic for heat, structural colour for biology-driven shifts.

buildSteps.title: Make the colour-changing material
buildSteps.detail: Electrochromic polymers are synthesised and cast into thin flexible films; photonic-crystal gels are assembled so their spacing — and therefore the wavelength they reflect — shifts when they swell.

buildSteps.title: Build the sensor
buildSteps.detail: For chemical triggers, an enzyme or aptamer that binds the target is immobilised next to the colour element, so binding produces a measurable signal.

buildSteps.title: Engineer biological versions
buildSteps.detail: Where living pigment cells are used, a gene circuit is inserted so that a chosen hormone or metabolite switches pigment production on or off. This has only been shown in cell culture, not in human skin.

buildSteps.title: Encapsulate
buildSteps.detail: The stack is sealed in a flexible, water-tight, biocompatible coating thin enough to sit in the dermis, since the body will otherwise wall it off with scar tissue.

buildSteps.title: Test in skin models
buildSteps.detail: Colour range, switching speed, toxicity and immune response are checked in cultured skin and animal models.

buildSteps.title: Place and calibrate
buildSteps.detail: The material is injected or pressed in with microneedles, then paired with an external reader and calibrated against known reference values.

buildSteps.title: Age and reliability testing
buildSteps.detail: The implant must keep working for months to years without fading, leaking or triggering inflammation.

prerequisites.why: these exist in smart windows and labels, but not yet in an implant-safe, flexible, long-lived form.
glucose-sensing tattoos and microneedle sensors have been demonstrated in the lab, not in routine use.

prerequisites.tech: Wireless power and data for implants
prerequisites.why: NFC coils already power and read small medical implants.
years-long tolerance in skin is the hardest unsolved problem for any subdermal device.
synthetic biology can make cells respond to specific molecules, but reliably linking that to something as vague as mood is not possible.

pathway.milestone: lab demonstrations of colour-changing tattoos that respond to blood glucose or pH, plus commercial electrochromic and thermochromic materials
pathway.unlocks: proof that a colour change can be read from the skin.

pathway.milestone: flexible, encapsulated subdermal devices with wireless control tested in animals
pathway.unlocks: safe placement in living tissue and remote command.

pathway.milestone: engineered pigment cells that switch colour under a specific chemical cue
clinically approved cosmetic implants with years-long stability
pathway.unlocks: genuinely programmable skin colour — most plausibly as medical or expressive cosmetics rather than mood reading, which no sensor can do reliably.
